text: RBAC grants access by assigning a user to a role, and that role works the same way every time, regardless of context. Attribute-based access control makes the decision differently: it evaluates a policy against a set of attributes at the moment of the request, and only grants access if those attributes satisfy the policy's conditions.

Where RBAC checks "does this user hold this role," ABAC checks the attributes themselves, fresh, every time a request comes in. A role can still exist underneath — ABAC doesn't require abandoning roles, it layers conditional logic on top of, or instead of, them.

A real ABAC policy draws on several kinds of attribute: user attributes like department or clearance level, resource attributes like a sensitivity label on a document, and environment attributes like time of day, network location, or whether the connecting device reports as compliant. A policy might read: Finance department users may read records tagged Confidential-Finance, during business hours, from a compliant managed device. Change any one condition and the access decision changes too.

Here's a case RBAC genuinely struggles with: a doctor should read a patient's record only if that patient is currently assigned to their care, and only during an active shift. Under RBAC that would take a separate role per doctor per shift — role explosion by another name. One ABAC policy expresses the real condition directly, evaluated per request.

That precision has a real cost. A role assignment is simple to audit — list the members, and that's the full answer. An ABAC policy is harder, because who can access a resource right now depends on evaluating attributes that can change minute to minute, like device compliance or location, not a static membership list. Reviewing ABAC access for a certification campaign means reasoning through policy logic, not reading a roster.

Both RBAC and ABAC assume the access being granted is ordinary, day-to-day access. Privileged access — the kind that can change security settings or touch every record in a system — needs its own discipline, which is where privileged access management picks up next.
